import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Erdős Problem 828

*Reference:* [erdosproblems.com/828](https://www.erdosproblems.com/828)
-/

namespace Erdos828

open scoped Nat

/--
Is it true that, for any $a \in \mathbb{Z}$, there are infinitely many $n$ such that
$$\phi(n) | n + a$$?
-/
@[category research open, AMS 11]
theorem erdos_828 : answer(sorry) ↔ ∀ a : ℤ, Set.Infinite {n : ℕ | ↑(φ n) ∣ n + a} := by
  sorry

/--
When $n > 1$, Lehmer conjectured that $\phi(n) | n - 1$ if and only if $n$ is prime.
-/
@[category research open, AMS 11]
theorem erdos_828.variants.lehmer_conjecture : answer(sorry) ↔ ∀ n > 1, φ n ∣ n - 1 ↔ Prime n := by
  sorry

/--
It is an easy exercise to show that $\phi(n) | n$ if and only if $n = 0, 1$ or $n = 2^a 3^b$ for
some $a > 0$.
-/
@[category textbook, AMS 11, formal_proof using formal_conjectures at
"https://github.com/XC0R/formal-conjectures/blob/03e00cf8d44098d0fb06e891fca30c29769df619/FormalConjectures/ErdosProblems/828.lean#L49"]
theorem erdos_828.variants.phi_dvd_self_iff_pow2_pow3 {n : ℕ} :
    φ n ∣ n ↔ n ≤ 1 ∨ ∃ᵉ (a > 0) (b), n = 2 ^ a * 3 ^ b := by
  sorry

end Erdos828

reformulations.difference: The set of solutions ranges over all natural numbers, including zero, rather than only positive integers.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: Removing zero, or any finite initial interval, preserves infinitude. Mathlib has φ(0)=0, so zero is a solution exactly when a=0; it cannot create an infinite solution set. Proved the equivalence with positive solutions, and more generally with solutions above any natural cutoff, in /workspace/review/scratch.lean.

reformulations.difference: The usual assertion that no composite number satisfies the divisibility condition is expressed as an iff with generic Prime, using natural-number subtraction and divisibility.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: On n>1, natural subtraction n-1 agrees with integer subtraction, and integer divisibility between natural-number casts agrees with natural divisibility. Nat.prime_iff identifies generic Prime with Nat.Prime. The prime-to-divisibility implication follows from φ(p)=p-1, so the iff is equivalent to asserting that every solution with n>1 is prime. Both equivalences were proved independently in the scratch file.

review.notes:
No mathematical defect found in the three declarations. Type inspection confirmed the integer arithmetic in the main question, correctly scoped propositional answer slots, and natural exponents with conjunctive existential bounds in the elementary variant. Boundary checks and finite tests through n=1000 passed; the equivalence proofs use no sorry axioms.

There is an evident source-side typo worth documenting: the website says φ(n) divides n iff n=2^a3^b for a,b≥0. Literally this is false at n=3. The file correctly uses a>0, handles n=1 separately, and adds the valid Mathlib boundary case n=0. This is a correction of the source typo, not an equivalence to its literal formula. Independently, Euler's product shows that a nontrivial solution must contain 2 and at most one odd prime; that odd prime, if present, must be 3. The Lean statement should not be changed to allow positive powers of 3 alone.

The reviewed file remained unchanged. The full Guy B37 text was unavailable; accessible snippets and the original Erdős–Dudley paper were consulted instead.
